The India-UK trade agreement, implemented in July, halved tariffs on Scotch to 75% . File | Photo Credit: The Hindu
India is imposing an effective duty of 162.5% on bulk Scotch imports amid an ongoing dispute over the India-UK trade agreement, raising concerns among liquor companies as the levy exceeds the 150% charged before the agreement, according to eight sources and a government document.
The India-UK trade agreement, implemented in July, halved tariffs on Scotch to 75%. Businesses and the British government had hailed the move as a major win for companies such as Pernod Ricard and Diageo, which import Scotch in bulk and blend it to make popular products for India’s USD 65-billion liquor market.
However, in the first major dispute linked to the trade agreement, Indian investigators have argued that companies are using incorrect customs classifications for bulk Scotch concentrates, which are treated as raw materials used to make drinks such as blended whiskies.
Since May, such imports have been classified under a newly created customs category for “compound alcoholic preparations”, which attracts a 150% t tariff, according to Indian investigators. These imports are then subject to a consumption tax, taking the total duty to 162.5% , according to a government document reviewed by Reuters and eight sources, including industry executives and customs agents familiar with the matter.
As the dispute continues, thousands of litres of bulk Scotch in more than 80 shipping containers belonging to Pernod, Diageo and Bacardi remain stuck at ports, Reuters reported last week.
Under a provisional release arrangement pending investigation, 75% of the goods’ value must be paid upfront, with the remaining amount covered by bank guarantees, the sources said.
“Industry has already reduced prices of Scotch products in the market when the India-UK pact kicked in, and now they are faced with higher duties again,” said a source in the liquor importing business.
Pernod, which owns UK-based Chivas Brothers, Diageo and several other Indian companies believe that both bulk and bottled Scotch imports should be taxed at 75% under the trade agreement.
The British government has repeatedly said in statements that it is working with New Delhi to resolve the issue, while India has said the dispute will be settled soon.
Pernod and Diageo have moved to arrange bank guarantees and other funding to secure the release of their blocked containers and ensure business continuity. Bacardi is still deciding its next steps, three of the sources said.
Shares of Diageo in London and Pernod in France fell following the Reuters report, declining 1.5% and 1.25%, respectively. India is Pernod’s biggest global market by volume, and the company, along with Diageo, dominates the Indian spirits market.
Diageo declined to comment, while Pernod and Bacardi did not respond to queries. The Indian Finance Ministry and the tax authority also did not respond.
Long-running tariff disputes have been a sore point for foreign investors and have affected companies such as Volkswagen and Samsung. Indian officials say they are only enforcing the law, but executives say they are often caught off guard by the way New Delhi classifies imports.
Mumbai-listed companies Radico Khaitan, Allied Blenders and Distillers, and Tilaknagar Industries also import bulk Scotch and are under scrutiny, along with Pernod and Diageo. Smaller companies could face greater pressure in arranging bank guarantees, as they may need to provide collateral. Such guarantees also have to be reported as contingent liabilities.
“We have no alternative at this stage,” said an Indian executive, referring to a possible disruption in the market due to a shortage of bulk Scotch. “Meeting the production requirements is extremely critical, even though bank guarantees stress working capital.”
About 80% of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume arrive in bulk, and India is the largest market for Scotch by volume.
Most bulk Scotch imports are used to make Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) whisky by blending a small quantity of Scotch with other spirits. These mass-market products are considerably cheaper than wholly imported whiskies such as Chivas Regal and Johnnie Walker.
Whisky tariffs were a sticking point during the years of negotiations leading up to the trade agreement’s implementation on July 15. Britain has said that “iconic UK products”, including whiskies, would benefit from the pact.
The UK’s Scotch Whisky Association has forecast that the trade agreement could boost Scotch exports to India by USD 1.34 billion over five years.
A confidential memo from Indian investigators, reported by Reuters last week, said that any misclassification under the India-UK trade agreement needed to stop as it had “substantial revenue implications” for New Delhi.
Indian liquor industry sources said that while the classification issue was being debated, they had not anticipated the imposition of the additional local tax.
“The local tax addition is a googly,” one industry source said, using the cricket term for a deceptive delivery by a bowler.
